title: The text that helped crack cuneiform was carved 100 metres up a cliff in Iran

cover.alt: A close view of the Behistun relief in Iran: King Darius I carved in profile on the cliff, with lines of cuneiform beside the figures.

body: Between 522 and 486 BC, Darius I had a life-size relief and the longest known trilingual cuneiform inscription cut into a limestone cliff at Behistun in western Iran, about 100 metres above an ancient road between Babylon and Ecbatana. The same account of how he took the throne appears in Old Persian, Elamite and Babylonian, which is what made it so important to the decipherment of cuneiform. In 1835 the British officer Henry Rawlinson began copying it, scaling the cliff with the help of a local boy, and in 1847 he sent a full, accurate copy to Europe. The site has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2006.

slides.label: up the cliff: the inscription’s height above the ancient road below
slides.text: The relief and panels together are about 15 m high and 25 m wide. In the text the Persian king Darius I says he fought nineteen battles in a single year to put down revolts.

slides.prompt: What damaged the monument in the 20th century?
slides.detail: Allied soldiers used it for target practice in the Second World War. Rainwater has also dissolved parts of the limestone.

slides.heading: Why it mattered
slides.text: Three versions of one text, side by side, made Behistun important to the decipherment of cuneiform. Old Persian, with only 37 signs, could be worked on first; Grotefend read 10 of them by 1802. In 1904 the British Museum’s Leonard King and Reginald Campbell Thompson added photographs, casts and better transcriptions.

slides.alt: Mount Behistun, a bare limestone mountain in Kermanshah Province, Iran, which carries the inscription high on its cliff face.
slides.caption: The inscription sits about 100 metres up this limestone cliff, above the ancient road from Babylon to Ecbatana.
